description: Team Kelvin367 is building a web app for "Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots": one consistent burning-activity calendar for any area, so emergency managers and land managers can compare fire seasons and spot unusual periods. We have a mathematician, a business analyst, a software engineer, an ML engineer and an Earth-science researcher. We need a UI/UX designer, a data-viz/front-end person and a storyteller to work on demo and pitch deck. We speak English and Ukrainian.
summary: Kelvin367 harmonizes NASA FIRMS active-fire detections from MODIS (Terra and Aqua) and VIIRS (S-NPP, NOAA-20, NOAA-21) into one comparable weekly record on the MODIS scale. Raw counts jump about three times when VIIRS replaces MODIS (Greece, 2012). That is an instrument effect, not a change in fire activity. We link the platforms in a calibration chain (NOAA-21 → NOAA-20 → S-NPP → MODIS) with separate day and night coefficients and an 80% uncertainty interval for every week. On held-out years 2022–2024 the disagreement between platforms fell from ×2.4–3.8 to ×1.25–1.46. A web app lets anyone pick an area in Europe, Africa or South America, switch between raw and harmonized series, and read the weekly calendar with its interval. App has following limits: the coefficient depends on the region (own coefficient for 10 areas, a rougher generalized one elsewhere), and the interval covered 78% of held-out weeks, not the nominal 80%.
details:
FIRMS publishes active-fire detections from two instrument families that do not count the same way: MODIS (1 km, 2000 onward) and VIIRS (375 m, 2012 onward). Anyone building a long fire record, or comparing years before and after 2012, meets a step that is not real. We built a harmonized weekly calendar of fire detections on one scale, with an uncertainty interval for every week.

(1) One definition of a detection for all platforms: acceptable confidence (MODIS ≥ 30, VIIRS nominal or high) and removal of persistent pixels (static sources such as industrial flares). (2) Weekly counts per platform, split into day and night, Terra and Aqua combined. (3) A calibration chain NOAA-21 → NOAA-20 → S-NPP → MODIS. Each link has a coefficient (geometric mean of the target/source ratio over overlap weeks) and a log-normal uncertainty by activity level, plus the variability of the coefficient between quarters. Where MODIS is available it is used as is; elsewhere VIIRS is converted through the chain. (4) The 80% interval was calibrated on 2020–2021 and tested on 2022 onward: pooled coverage 78%, from 66% to 89% across areas.

Benefits and impact. Comparable records across the 2012 instrument change and across platform generations, including the end of S-NPP delivery, for research, insurance, emergency planning and trip and logistics planning.

Limits. The coefficient depends on the burning regime (2.1× spread by day, 3.2× by night between areas). Ten areas have their own coefficient; the rest of Europe, Africa and South America use a generalized one with bias up to ±50%. We harmonize counts, not individual detections, and not FRP or brightness temperature.

Tools. Python (pandas, NumPy, PyArrow) for processing; a static web app in plain JavaScript without third-party libraries; NASA FIRMS API for data; AWS Amplify for hosting.

Creativity and factors considered. The uncertainty interval is part of the product rather than an afterthought. We tested the method on held-out years and on ten areas across four continents, and report where it is weaker.

Beyond the challenge, we tested whether harmonized data give a better one-week-ahead fire forecast than raw data. Trained only for Spain, 3 days ahead forecast is available in the app forecast tab at https://kelvin-firemap-a4gne7c7gueudeak.westeurope-01.azurewebsites.net/
